source.title: Alignment Whack-a-Mole : Finetuning Activates Verbatim Recall of Copyrighted Books in Large Language Models
source.authors: Xin-Yue Liu; Niloofar Mireshghallah; Jane C. Ginsburg; Tuhin Chakrabarty

page_placements.theme: Adaptation changes privacy, fairness and other values beyond refusal

record.file_problem: None; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses fine-tuning as a way to bypass copyright-related output safeguards, but its own experiments measure verbatim copyright recall, not harmful-request refusals, KL across response positions, or the other behaviors named in V1–V7. Its safety-alignment claims are background citations, not results from this study.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Qi et al. (2023) for safety-alignment compromise, but does not reproduce or test those findings. Its own results concern copyright extraction, a related but different construct; the aggregate copyright-recall measurements are recorded under fits_no_version. The paper also reports many per-book and per-model copyright results, which are not enumerated here because none measures a claim version. It reports some results only in figures, including parts of the public-domain-versus-synthetic and Llama stage comparisons.
record.test_reason: The study measures verbatim reproduction of copyrighted books (bmc@5, span lengths) after plot-to-text fine-tuning. It does not measure harmful-request compliance, per-token KL, prefilling or suffix attacks, parameter localization or deepening training. Qi et al. (2023) is cited only as motivation. The behaviour bypassed is a copyright guardrail, not refusal of harmful requests, so this is a related but different construct. No V1–V7 version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that plot-summary-to-text fine-tuning makes GPT-4o, Gemini-2.5-Pro and DeepSeek-V3.1 reproduce large verbatim portions of held-out copyrighted books, including books by authors absent from fine-tuning. They attribute this to reactivated pretraining memorization: public-domain data works, synthetic data does not. They report that the three models memorize the same regions (r ≥ 0.90). They argue that alignment, RLHF and output filters suppress but do not remove this risk, with implications for fair-use rulings.
record.recipe_differences: The study fine-tunes models to expand plot summaries into verbatim book text and measures copyright recall; it does not apply the harmful-example or benign-instruction safety fine-tuning recipes in the cited original safety study, nor the response-position KL measurement in the other original source.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports variation by fine-tuning data type and pretraining overlap: public-domain Woolf data gives extraction comparable to the cross-author condition, while synthetic data gives marginal bmc@5 gains and virtually no long verbatim spans. It also notes that Gemini-2.5-Pro output filters lower some results.

fits_no_version.finding: Fine-tuning frontier models to expand plot summaries into text raises verbatim recall of held-out copyrighted books over the aligned GPT-4o reference. Aggregate bmc@5 is 35.24 within-author and 48.54 cross-author, against chance floors of 0.90 and 11.10.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Narrow, benign-looking fine-tuning bypasses alignment-based copyright guardrails and reactivates memorized pretraining text.

fits_no_version.finding: Llama-3.1-405B base reaches up to 92.0 bmc@5. Instruction tuning lowers this to 10.5–24.5, and Murakami LoRA fine-tuning of the instruct model restores it to 49.7–80.3 (Figure 4). The authors say alignment 'hides memorization rather than removing it'.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Alignment suppresses verbatim recall superficially; fine-tuning restores base-model behaviour (a copyright analogue of shallow alignment).

fits_no_version.finding: Fine-tuning on public-domain Woolf text gives extraction comparable to Murakami fine-tuning on The Handmaid's Tale. Fine-tuning on synthetic SimpleStories gives only marginal bmc@5 gains and almost no long spans (Figure 3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Recovery of suppressed behaviour after fine-tuning depends on overlap between the fine-tuning data and pretraining data.

record.problems: The aligned-model baseline uses GPT-4o only because inference on more than 80 books was costly; the authors say preliminary tests indicated similar behavior for Gemini-2.5-Pro and DeepSeek-V3.1. Several comparisons are described qualitatively or presented in figures, and the recorded aggregate fine-tuning means are not paired with an aggregate baseline for the same exact book sets.
record.rows_left_out: Per-book and per-model copyright extraction results in Figures 2–4 and Tables 7–8, plus additional copyright-related analyses, are not enumerated because they do not measure any V1–V7 behavior. Figure-only comparisons are also omitted; see §4, Figures 2–4, and Tables 7–8.

untested.parts: Harmful-example fine-tuning and harmful-request compliance: not measured.
Benign fine-tuning raising harmful-request compliance: not measured. Only copyright recall after benign-looking fine-tuning is measured.
Per-token KL between aligned and base models across response positions: not measured.
Prefilling, adversarial suffixes and decoding changes against refusal: not tested.
Localization of safety in few weights or ranks: not tested. LoRA rank 32 is used only as a fine-tuning tool.
Cause of shallowness in data or objective: not tested.
Deepening training and its robustness: not tested.

record.verdict_notes: Gate: the paper frames fine-tuning as bypassing 'safety alignment', but its alignment target is copyright non-regurgitation, not refusal of harmful requests, so it does not test any version. The Llama base/instruct/fine-tuned comparison is the closest analogue to the shallow-alignment idea, but it concerns a different behaviour; it is recorded under fits_no_version. The rows' baselines are not matched to the same book subsets, and the aligned baseline is GPT-4o only.

versions.untested_parts: Harmful-request compliance after benign instruction fine-tuning.
Per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models on harmful prompts.
Compliant opening prefills, suffixes, decoding changes, and harmful-request refusal.
Whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behavior.
Whether the data or training objective causes safety shallowness.
Training to deepen safety and its robustness.

rows.check: This is a reference measurement of the unfinetuned aligned GPT-4o (bmc@5 7.36), not an effect, so 'observed' has no meaning. Note also that the paper's own chance floor for generations scored against unrelated books (Table 6, mean 11.10) exceeds this baseline. Readers should not treat 7.36 as above chance.

relation.reason: The introduction and related work discuss safety degradation through fine-tuning as motivation; the study neither tests the listed versions nor uses their findings as an experimental tool.

tranche.reason: The experiments measure copyrighted-book extraction, a different construct from the harmful compliance and safety mechanisms named by V1–V7.

source_check.notes: The statement accurately names GPT-4o as a reference, but its aggregate comparisons are unmatched. Chance floors 0.90 and 11.10 denote unrelated book–book and book–generation controls, respectively, not separate within-author and cross-author floors.
